Downtime

Storytellers use "downtime" between sessions to let characters maintain holdings, learn Disciplines, and handle other facets of their unlife that don't make for dramatic in-session roleplaying. Other actions and interactions may also take place during downtime, with Storyteller supervision.

Health Levels

A character has a track of health levels representing how much injury she can endure, in order: Healthy, Healthy, Bruised, Bruised, Bruised, Wounded, Wounded, Incapacitated, then Torpor (from lethal damage) or Final Death (from aggravated damage). Losing two health levels moves a Healthy character to Bruised; three more levels of loss moves her to Wounded, and so on.

  • Healthy: Virtually or completely uninjured. No penalty beyond cosmetic scuffs.
  • Bruised: Visibly roughed up. The character is one Trait down on all tied challenges.
  • Wounded: Seriously injured. The character must risk an additional Trait to attempt a challenge, and her opponent automatically wins all ties (even powers that normally let the wounded character win ties instead fall back to comparing Traits). The wounded character may still attempt to overbid.
  • Incapacitated: Completely out of play for at least 10 minutes. Once conscious, the character is still immobile and can only whisper pained sentences; she cannot enter challenges until she heals at least one health level, and can do nothing but heal herself. A Kindred who suffers aggravated damage while Incapacitated meets Final Death.
  • Torpor: Kindred pushed past Incapacitated by lethal damage fall into a deathlike sleep.
  • Final Death: Kindred pushed past Incapacitated by aggravated damage are permanently destroyed, rather than entering torpor.

Bashing vs. Lethal Damage

Bashing damage is painful but fades quickly — kicks, punches, tackles. Lethal damage (bullets, blades, etc.) is meant to kill and takes mortals a long time to heal. The Narrator has final say on what counts as which. Mortals and creatures pushed below Incapacitated by bashing damage are merely knocked unconscious for one scene/hour (Narrators may rule torpor or death for an especially brutal beating); mortals pushed below Incapacitated by lethal damage die, while vampires enter torpor.

Because Cainites' corpselike bodies don't bruise and break like the bodies of the living, vampires halve all bashing damage received, rounding down (minimum one level inflicted).

Aggravated Wounds

Wounds beyond the reach of a Kindred's normal regenerative power are aggravated — typically caused by fire, sunlight, or the teeth and claws of supernatural creatures (a Narrator may also rule other injuries aggravated). Healing one level of aggravated damage costs three Blood Traits, one Willpower Trait, and a night of rest.

Sunlight

Indirect sunlight (through thick curtains, heavy cloud cover) inflicts one automatic aggravated wound per turn of exposure; direct sunlight inflicts three automatic levels of aggravated damage per turn (heavy clothing may grant some protection, Storyteller's discretion). Vampires confronted by sunlight must also make a Static Courage Challenge or suffer Rötschreck.

Fire

All wounds from normal or magical fire inflict aggravated damage on Kindred, and a sufficiently large flame provokes a Courage Test against Rötschreck. A character on fire must win or tie a Simple Test and spend an action dousing the flames.

Healing with Blood

Vampires are dead and cannot heal naturally; only their own vitae repairs damage. One Blood Trait heals one health level of lethal damage, or two health levels of bashing damage. Healing this way can be performed alongside other actions, even Discipline use, but requires concentration and a full turn, and is still bound by the character's generation limits on blood expenditure per turn (so most young vampires can't heal more than one health level in a single turn).

Torpor

Characters may enter torpor voluntarily or involuntarily (wounds or other causes). A character with no Blood Traits left loses a health level each time the rules call for her to spend blood (such as at sunset); falling below Incapacitated this way also causes torpor. Length of involuntary torpor depends on the character's Humanity rating:

Humanity TraitsLength of Torpor
5Two days
4One week
3One year
2One decade
1One century
0One millennium

After the required rest, the character may attempt a Static Mental Challenge against three Traits and expend a Blood Trait to wake. Failure allows another attempt once per night until she succeeds or runs out of blood; with no blood at all, she cannot rise until someone gives her blood. Voluntary torpor (a deeper version of the daily rest) allows waking in half the chart's time, still requiring the Static Mental Challenge. Torpid vampires do not need nightly blood — they are effectively hibernating.

Movement in Combat

Three Step Rule

Anyone in or entering combat may take up to three steps during a combat action and still attack. One step is walking cautiously (no penalty). Two steps is moving directly, and three steps is running — both put the character down one Trait on Physical Challenges that turn. A Discipline granting an additional action grants three additional steps as well, and so on.

Fair Escape

Fair Escape lets a player leave a potentially dangerous situation without an extended chase or combat challenge. Calling "Fair Escape!" when another player approaches whom you don't wish to interact with lets you leave the area without pursuit, subject to limits:

  • Cannot be used if the approaching character is already within conversational distance — a challenge must be initiated to flee instead. (Use common sense in loud environments where conversational distance shrinks, like a nightclub.)
  • An ambush (all exits blocked, target surrounded) or ranged weapons can negate Fair Escape at Narrator discretion.
  • A character using Unseen Presence or similar powers may Fair Escape any time before a challenge starts, unless countered by Heightened Senses.
  • Characters with supernatural speed (e.g. Celerity) gain a Fair Escape by activating their speed before a challenge begins; if both sides have supernatural speed, the higher level wins (ties favor the fleeing party) — Basic Celerity cannot Fair Escape from Advanced Celerity.

Surprise

If a player doesn't respond within three seconds of a Physical Challenge being declared, her character is surprised. The outcome of that first challenge can only harm the surprised defender — a challenger who wins inflicts the agreed result, but a challenger who loses inflicts nothing on herself and may call for a second challenge by risking another Trait, after which normal challenge rules resume. Overbidding is allowed for both sides in a surprise situation. Sneaking around whispering challenges purely to engineer surprise is considered cheating.
